sites.status: Mission failed — spacecraft impacted the Moon
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: Approximate impact location published in NASA NSSDCA anthropogenic impacts table; not imaged by LROC.
sites.summary: The first Ranger to reach the Moon — it missed its target by 370 km and struck the surface without returning close-up pictures.
narrative: Ranger 3 launched on 26 January 1962 to photograph the lunar surface before impact. A guidance error sent it 370 km past its aim point, and on 28 January it struck the Moon at about 10.4 degrees north, 20.2 degrees west, without returning useful images.

The spacecraft remains where it struck, buried or scattered in the impact debris. It is listed in NASA's Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon and the NSSDCA Table of Anthropogenic Impacts, which records its approximate impact coordinates.

sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)

sites.summary: Ranger 5 lost power hours after launch and fell to the Moon silent, becoming one of the earliest human-made objects left on another world.
narrative: Ranger 5 launched on 21 June 1962. A battery failure silenced the spacecraft within hours, and it continued on a trajectory that brought it to impact the Moon later that day at about 12.6 degrees north, 39.3 degrees west.
No images were returned. The spacecraft is catalogued by NASA as manmade material on the Moon, its wreckage still lying in the region it struck.

sites.summary: The last Ranger before the successful Ranger 7–9 series — it struck the Moon at about 19.8 N, 10.5 W after its camera failed.
narrative: Ranger 10 launched on 25 March 1965 as a Block III Ranger. Its television camera failed shortly after launch, so when it impacted the Moon that day at about 19.8 degrees north, 10.5 degrees west, it returned no close-up images.
The spacecraft remains at its impact site, listed in NASA's lunar artefacts catalogue alongside the later, successful Rangers 7, 8 and 9.

sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: Impact location from Ksanfomality (2018) as cited by NSSDCA; other published estimates differ by several degrees, hence approximate.
sites.summary: The Soviet Union's first attempt at a soft lunar landing — Luna 5 crashed at 1.35 S, 25.48 W and was left where it fell.
narrative: Luna 5 launched on 9 May 1965 to attempt the first soft landing on the Moon. Its braking engine fired late, and on 12 May the lander struck the surface at about 1.35 degrees south, 25.48 degrees west, in the Mare Serenitatis region.

The wreckage remains there. NASA NSSDCA lists the impact coordinates from Ksanfomality (2018) and notes that other published estimates differ, so the position is shown as approximate rather than surveyed.

sites.summary: Luna 7's parachute failed and the lander hit the Moon at 9 N, 49 W — another Soviet attempt left in the dust.
narrative: Luna 7 launched on 4 October 1965. During descent its parachute system failed, and on 7 October the lander impacted the Moon at about 9 degrees north, 49 degrees west.
The spacecraft remains at the impact site, catalogued by NASA NSSDCA among the anthropogenic impacts on the Moon.

sites.summary: Luna 8 aimed to land near Luna 7's wreck and instead joined it, impacting at 9.1 N, 63.3 W.
narrative: Luna 8 launched on 3 December 1965 to attempt a soft landing in Oceanus Procellarum. Its descent failed, and on 6 December the lander impacted at about 9.1 degrees north, 63.3 degrees west.
The spacecraft remains where it struck. NASA NSSDCA lists its approximate impact coordinates in the table of anthropogenic impacts on the Moon.

sites.status: Mission failed — lander impacted the Moon
sites.coordSystem: Mean Earth/Polar Axis lunar frame, planetocentric (DE421)
sites.coordNote: NSSDCA lists Surveyor 4 location as unknown, estimated near 0.5 N, 1.5 W from trajectory analysis; possibly fragmented. Shown as uncertain.
sites.summary: Surveyor 4 went silent 2.5 minutes before landing and is thought to have crashed near Sinus Medii — its exact resting place is still unknown.
narrative: Surveyor 4 launched on 14 June 1967 to land in Sinus Medii. Contact was lost about 2.5 minutes before touchdown, and the spacecraft is thought to have impacted at about 0.5 degrees north, 1.5 degrees west, possibly in fragments.

NASA NSSDCA lists the location as unknown with that estimate, and the Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon records Surveyor 4 as UNKNOWN. The marker is therefore shown as uncertain — the spacecraft is somewhere in that area, but no one has imaged it.

sites.summary: Japan's Hiten orbited the Moon for over a year, then was deliberately crashed at 34 S, 55.3 E in 1993.
narrative: Hiten, launched by Japan's Institute of Space and Astronautical Science in 1990, became the first lunar orbiter from outside the United States and Soviet Union. After more than a year in lunar orbit, it was intentionally impacted on 10 April 1993 at about 34 degrees south, 55.3 degrees east.
The spacecraft remains at its impact site, listed by NASA NSSDCA in the table of anthropogenic impacts on the Moon.

sites.summary: Europe's SMART-1 tested solar-electric propulsion around the Moon, then ended its mission with a controlled impact at 34.4 S, 46.2 W.
narrative: SMART-1, the European Space Agency's first lunar mission, launched in 2003 and used solar-electric propulsion to reach the Moon in 2006. After mapping the surface, it was intentionally impacted on 3 September 2006 at about 34.4 degrees south, 46.2 degrees west.
The spacecraft remains at its impact site in the Lacus Excellentiae region, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

narrative: Chang'e 1 launched in October 2007 and became China's first lunar orbiter, producing a complete map of the lunar surface. On 1 March 2009 it was intentionally impacted at about 1.5 degrees south, 52.36 degrees east.
The spacecraft remains at its impact site, listed by NASA NSSDCA among the anthropogenic impacts on the Moon.

The spacecraft remains at its impact site, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

narrative: Chang'e 2 launched in October 2010 to select a landing site for Chang'e 3, mapping the Moon at higher resolution than Chang'e 1. On 8 October 2010 it was intentionally impacted at about 28.2 degrees north, 26.4 degrees west.
The spacecraft remains at its impact site, catalogued by NASA NSSDCA as an anthropogenic impact on the Moon.

sites.summary: China's first Moon landing — Chang'e 3 touched down in Sinus Iridum in 2013 and is still there, imaged by LROC.
narrative: Chang'e 3 landed on 14 December 2013 at 44.1214 degrees north, 19.5117 degrees west in Sinus Iridum, Mare Imbrium — China's first soft landing on the Moon. It deployed the Yutu rover, which operated for several weeks.
The lander remains on the surface. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images show the lander and rover tracks at the site, as recorded in NASA NSSDCA's table and LROC Featured Sites.

sites.summary: Yutu, China's first lunar rover, drove from Chang'e 3 in 2013 and stopped in Sinus Iridum, where it remains.
narrative: Yutu was deployed from the Chang'e 3 lander on 14 December 2013 and became China's first lunar rover. It drove across the surface of Sinus Iridum at 44.1208 degrees north, 19.5122 degrees west, before its mobility failed.
The rover remains where it stopped. LROC images show its tracks and final position near the lander, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

sites.summary: Beresheet, the first privately funded Moon landing attempt, crashed at 32.5956 N, 19.3496 E in 2019 and was imaged by LROC.
narrative: Beresheet, built by the Israeli non-profit SpaceIL, launched in February 2019 as the first privately funded attempt to land on the Moon. During its landing burn on 11 April 2019 the main engine failed, and the lander impacted at 32.5956 degrees north, 19.3496 degrees east.
Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images show the impact site and debris. The spacecraft remains there, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images later identified the impact site and debris. The lander remains there, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

sites.summary: Chang'e 5 landed near Mons Rümker in 2020, collected lunar samples and returned them to Earth — the lander itself is still there.
narrative: Chang'e 5 landed on 1 December 2020 at 43.0576 degrees north, 51.9161 degrees west near Mons Rümker in Oceanus Procellarum. It collected lunar samples and its ascent craft returned them to Earth, the first lunar sample return since Luna 24 in 1976.
The lander remains on the surface. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images show the lander at the site, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

narrative: Hakuto-R Mission 1, built by the Japanese company ispace, attempted to land on the Moon on 25 April 2023. During descent its altitude calculation failed, and the lander impacted at 47.581 degrees north, 44.094 degrees east.
Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images show the impact site and debris. The lander remains there, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA.

sites.summary: Japan's SLIM lander touched down in Shioli Crater in 2024, demonstrating precision landing — it sits at 13.316 S, 25.251 E.
narrative: SLIM, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, landed on 19 January 2024 at 13.316 degrees south, 25.251 degrees east in Shioli Crater, Mare Nectaris. It demonstrated precision landing using image matching, touching down within tens of metres of its target.

The lander remains on the surface. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images show SLIM at the site, as recorded by NASA NSSDCA. It is classified as a landing location (blue) because it completed its demonstration mission on the surface.

sites.summary: NASA lists the Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe impact near Shackleton crater at estimated coordinates; the exact location is unknown.
narrative: The Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe (MIP) impacted near Shackleton crater on 14 November 2008. NASA NSSDCA lists an estimated position of 89 degrees south, 30 degrees west, citing the published mission analysis.
